questions.question: What does the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach about christ the mediator?
questions.reference_answer: It pleased God in his eternal purpose, to chuse and ordain the Lord Jesus his only begotten Son, according to the Covenant made between them both, to be the Mediator between God and Man; the Prophet, Priest and King; Head and Saviour of his Church, the heir of all things, and judge of the world: Unto whom he did from all Eternity give a people to be his seed, and to be by him in time redeemed, called, justified, sanctified, and glorified. The Son of God, the second Person in the Holy Trinity, being very and eternal God, the brightness of the Fathers glory, of one substance and equal with him: who made the World, who upholdeth and governeth all things he hath made: did when the fullness of time was come take unto him mans nature, with all the Essential properties, and common infirmities thereof, yet without sin: being conceived by the Holy Spirit in the Womb of the Virgin Mary, the Holy Spirit coming down upon her, and the power of the most High overshadowing her, and so was made of a Woman, of the Tribe of Judah, of the Seed of Abraham, and David according to the Scriptures: So that two whole, perfect, and distinct natures, were inseparably joined together in one Person: without conversion, composition, or confusion: which Person is very God, and very Man; yet one Christ, the only Mediator between God and Man. The Lord Jesus in his humane nature thus united to the divine, in the Person of the Son, was sanctified, and anointed with the Holy Spirit, above measure; having in him all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge; in whom it pleased the Father that all fullness should dwell: To the end that being holy, harmless, undefiled, and full of Grace, and Truth, he might be throughly furnished to execute the office of a Mediator, and Surety; which office he took not upon himself, but was thereunto called by his Father; who also put all power and judgement in his hand, and gave him Commandement to execute the same. This office the Lord Jesus did most willingly undertake, which that he might discharge he was made under the Law, and did perfectly fulfill it, and underwent the punishment due to us, which we should have born and suffered, being made Sin and a Curse for us: enduring most grievous sorrows in his Soul; and most painful sufferings in his body; was crucified, and died, and remained in the state of the dead; yet saw no corruption: on the third day he arose from the dead, with the same body in which he suffered; with which he also ascended into heaven: and there sitteth at the right hand of his Father, making intercession; and shall return to judge Men and Angels, at the end of the World. The Lord Jesus by his perfect obedience and sacrifice of himself, which he through the Eternal Spirit once offered up unto God, hath fully satisfied the Justice of God, procured reconciliation, and purchased an Everlasting inheritance in the Kingdom of Heaven, for all those whom the Father hath given unto him. Although the price of Redemption was not actually paid by Christ, till after his Incarnation, yet the vertue, efficacy, and benefit thereof were communicated to the Elect in all ages successively, from the beginning of the World, in and by those Promises, Types, and Sacrifices, wherein he was revealed, and signified to be the Seed of the Woman, which should bruise the Serpents head; and the Lamb slain from the foundation of the World: Being the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever. Christ in the work of Mediation acteth according to both natures, by each nature doing that which is proper to it self; yet by reason of the Unity of the Person, that which is proper to one nature, is sometimes in Scripture attributed to the Person denominated by the other nature. To all those for whom Christ hath obtained eternal redemption, he doth certainly, and effectually apply, and communicate the same; making intercession for them, uniting them to himself by his spirit, revealing unto them, in and by the word, the mystery of salvation; perswading them to believe, and obey; governing their hearts by his word and spirit, and overcoming all their enemies by his Almighty power, and wisdom; in such manner, and wayes as are most consonant to his wonderful, and unsearchable dispensation; and all of free, and absolute Grace, without any condition foreseen in them, to procure it. This office of Mediator between God and Man, is proper onely to Christ, who is the Prophet, Priest, and King of the Church of God; and may not be either in whole, or any part thereof transfer'd from him to any other. This number and order of Offices is necessary; for in respect of our ignorance, we stand in need of his prophetical Office; and in respect of our alienation from God, and imperfection of the best of our services, we need his Priestly office, to reconcile us, and present us acceptable unto God: and in respect our averseness, and utter inability to return to God, and for our rescue, and security from our spiritual adversaries, we need his Kingly office, to convince, subdue, draw, uphold, deliver, and preserve us to his Heavenly Kingdome.

*   They are kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation.
*   The certainty of this perseverance is absolute, guaranteeing they will certainly endure to the end and be saved.

### 2. Believers May Fall into Serious Sin, But Not Total Apostasy
The Confession makes a critical distinction between falling into sin and falling away from grace. It acknowledges that Christians are capable of significant moral failures.
*   **Paragraph 2:** Saints may "fall into grievous sins" and continue in them for a time due to the temptations of Satan and the corruption remaining in their flesh.
*   **Consequences:** These sins bring God’s displeasure, grieve the Holy Spirit, and often result in the believer being deprived of some comforts and assurances of faith. Their hearts may be hardened, and their consciences wounded.
*   **The Result:** However, they will not totally fall from grace. God will renew them to repentance through the ministry of the Word and discipline within the church.

### 3. God Uses Means to Preserve Them
Perseverance is not a passive state where the believer does nothing; rather, God actively preserves them through specific means.
*   **Paragraph 3:** God preserves the saints through the use of the "means of grace." These include:

While there are similarities with the Lutheran view, the Reformed perspective places a unique emphasis on the continuity of God’s redemptive plan and the ongoing usefulness of the Law for the believer.

The Reformed view can be summarized by three main principles: **strict distinction**, **necessary unity**, and the **three uses of the Law**.

### 1. The Fundamental Distinction
Reformed theology insists that the Law and the Gospel must be clearly distinguished, though never separated. This is often framed as a distinction between "Do" and "Done."

*   **The Law ("Do this"):** The Law represents God's holy demands. It is the command to perfect obedience. It says, "Do this and you will live" (Leviticus 18:5; Luke 10:28). It functions as a covenant of works: if you obey perfectly, you are blessed; if you disobey, you are cursed.
*   **The Gospel ("Done this"):** The Gospel represents God's gracious provision. It is the announcement of what Christ has done. It says, "Believe and you will live" (John 3:16; Romans 1:16). It is a covenant of grace: salvation is a free gift received by faith alone, not by works.

The doctrine of original sin is the theological belief that humanity inherits a sinful nature and a propensity to sin as a result of the Fall of Adam and Eve. While the specific phrase "original sin" does not appear in the Bible, the concept is derived from several passages that describe the universal nature of sin, its origin in Adam, and the inherited corruption of the human heart.

Here are the primary Scripture passages used to teach this doctrine, categorized by their specific contribution to the theology.

### 1. The Origin: The Fall in Genesis
The foundation of the doctrine is found in the narrative of Adam and Eve, where sin enters the human experience, resulting in spiritual and physical death.

*   **Genesis 2:17:** "But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die."
    *   *Significance:* God established the covenant of life with Adam, with death as the penalty for disobedience.
*   **Genesis 3:** The account of the disobedience (The Fall).
    *   *Significance:* This historical event is viewed as the moment sin and death entered the world, affecting all of creation.

### 2. The Inherited Nature: We are Born Sinners
These passages indicate that we are not sinners merely because we sin, but that we sin because we are born with a sinful nature.

*   **Psalm 51:5:** "Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me."
    *   *Significance:* King David acknowledges that his sinfulness extends back to the very moment of his conception, suggesting an inherited moral corruption rather than a learned behavior.
*   **Psalm 58:3:** "The wicked are estranged from the womb; they go astray from birth, speaking lies."

questions.response:
The doctrine of the imputation of Christ’s righteousness teaches that the perfect obedience and holiness of Jesus Christ are credited to the account of the believer. While the specific phrase "imputation of Christ’s righteousness" does not appear verbatim in the Bible, the concept is taught explicitly through the use of accounting and legal terminology (specifically the Greek word *logizomai*, meaning "to reckon," "count," or "impute").

Here are the primary passages where this doctrine is found:

### 1. 2 Corinthians 5:21 (The "Great Exchange")
This is perhaps the most direct statement of the doctrine in all of Scripture. It describes a double imputation: our sin being placed on Christ, and His righteousness being placed on us.

> **"He made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in Him."**

*   **The Teaching:** Christ, who was personally sinless, was treated as sinful by God on the cross (bearing the penalty for sin). In exchange, believers (who are sinful) are treated as righteous in union with Christ. The righteousness we become is not our own internal goodness, but "the righteousness of God" found "in Him."

### 2. Romans 4:3–8 (The Logic of Imputation)
In Romans 4, the Apostle Paul explains how justification works by looking at Abraham. He uses the Greek word *logizomai* repeatedly (translated as "counted," "reckoned," or "imputed") to explain that righteousness is a status granted by God, not a wage earned by works.

> **"For what does the Scripture say? 'Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.'"** (v. 3)

Paul clarifies that this righteousness is not something Abraham earned through behavior, but something credited to him by faith. He extends this to believers in verse 5:

> **"But to him who does not work but believes on Him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is accounted for righteousness."**

Paul then connects this to David in verses 6–8, describing the blessedness of the man "to whom God imputes righteousness apart from works."

This passage provides the theological structural basis for imputation. Paul contrasts Adam (the representative of humanity) with Christ (the representative of the new humanity).

Here is a breakdown of where the Bible teaches about the final judgment, categorized by section and key passages.

### 1. The Old Testament (Foundations)
While the Old Testament focuses heavily on God’s judgment of nations in history, it also looks forward to a final, cosmic "Day of the Lord."

*   **Daniel 12:1-2:** This is perhaps the clearest Old Testament reference to a final resurrection and judgment. *   **Ecclesiastes 12:14:** Solomon writes, *"For God will bring every deed into judgment, including every hidden thing, whether it is good or evil."*

### 2. The Gospels (The Teachings of Jesus)

*   **Matthew 25:31-46 (The Sheep and the Goats):** This is the most vivid narrative of the judgment in the Gospels. Here are the primary biblical passages and confessional standards that address the sacraments in Reformed theology, categorized by their theological function.

### 1. The Definition and Nature of Sacraments

    *   *Significance:* Establishes the continuity of the covenant community and the use of visible signs for inclusion in God's people.

questions.response:
From a Reformed theological perspective, the statement **"God's saving grace can be ultimately resisted by the free will of man" is false.**

This statement represents the core of the Arminian view of predestination and stands in direct opposition to the Reformed doctrine of **Irresistible Grace** (often called "Efficacious Grace").

Here is a detailed evaluation of why this statement is rejected by Reformed theology, categorized by key doctrinal distinctives.

### 1. The Doctrine of Irresistible Grace
Reformed theology is famously summarized by the acronym TULIP. The "I" stands for **Irresistible Grace**.

*   **The Reformed Position:** Reformed theologians argue that when God calls a person to salvation (the "effectual call"), that call cannot be thwarted. It is not that God drags someone kicking and screaming against their will; rather, the Holy Spirit changes the human heart's disposition so that the person *willingly* and *freely* desires Christ.
*   **The Evaluation:** The statement in question suggests that God’s grace is a mere offer that depends on the human recipient to make it effective. Reformed theology contends that saving grace is effective by definition. If it can be resisted and ultimately fail, it is not "saving" grace in the ultimate sense, but merely "common" grace or a temporary influence.

### 2. The Spiritual Inability of Man (Total Depravity)
To understand why Reformed theology rejects the idea that man can resist saving grace, one must look to the "T" in TULIP: **Total Depravity**.

*   **The Reformed Position:** This doctrine teaches that as a result of the Fall, humanity is spiritually dead. Apart from the regenerating work of the Holy Spirit, human beings are morally unable to choose God. They are not just sick or injured; they are spiritually corpses (Ephesians 2:1-5).
*   **The Evaluation:** The statement implies that man possesses a "free will" that is neutral and capable of accepting or rejecting God. Reformed theology argues that the unregenerate will is not free; it is enslaved to sin. Therefore, a person cannot "resist" grace in the sense of holding back a power that is trying to save them; rather, they are hostile to God until God intervenes to change their nature.     *   This is based on the doctrine of **Imputed Righteousness**. Christ’s perfect obedience to the Law and His atoning death are credited (imputed) to the believer’s account. The believer does not become inherently righteous in this act; rather, they are *declared* legally righteous because of Christ.

questions.response:
The differences between Reformed and Roman Catholic views on the sacraments are rooted in a broader disagreement about the nature of grace, authority, and the Church. While both traditions are "sacramental"—meaning they believe God uses physical elements to convey spiritual truth—they differ significantly on **how** that happens, **how many** sacraments there are, and **what** the sacraments actually do.

Here is a breakdown of the key differences.

### 1. The Number of Sacraments
The most immediate difference is quantity.

*   **Roman Catholic:** Recognizes **seven** sacraments: Baptism, Confirmation (Chrismation), Eucharist, Penance (Reconciliation), Anointing of the Sick, Holy Orders, and Matrimony.
*   **Reformed:** Recognizes **two** sacraments: Baptism and the Lord’s Supper.

**The Reasoning:** The Reformed view follows the "Regulative Principle of Worship," which holds that only institutions explicitly commanded by Christ and practiced by the early apostolic church should be observed. Since only Baptism and the Lord’s Supper were instituted by Christ with a specific divine command and promise, the Reformed tradition classifies the other five (like marriage or last rites) as "rites" or "ordinances" that are good and beneficial, but not distinct "means of grace" in the same theological category.

### 2. The Mechanism of Grace (How they work)
This is the theological heart of the division.

*   **Roman Catholic (Ex Opere Operato):** Catholic theology teaches that the sacraments work *ex opere operato* ("from the work performed"). This means that the sacrament is effective by virtue of the act itself, provided it is performed by a validly ordained priest with the correct intention and matter. The grace is conferred objectively; the personal holiness or faith of the recipient is not required for the sacrament to be valid (though it is required for the fruit of the sacrament to be received).
*   **Reformed (Means of Grace):** The Reformed view teaches that the sacraments are "means of grace." They do not work automatically (like magic). Instead, they are effective only through the power of the Holy Spirit and are received by **faith**. A sacrament without faith is a "dead letter." The signs (water, bread, wine) do not become grace automatically but confirm and seal God's promises to the believer who trusts in them.

questions.response:
The difference between Reformed and Roman Catholic views on Scripture and tradition is one of the most significant divides in Christian theology. It fundamentally comes down to the question of **authority**: Where do we look for the final rule of faith and practice?

Here is a breakdown of the differences across four key categories.

### 1. The Source of Authority (The Material Principle)

**Reformed View: *Sola Scriptura* (Scripture Alone)**
The Reformed tradition holds that Scripture alone is the ultimate authority for the church.
*   **Sufficiency:** Scripture contains everything necessary for God’s glory and human salvation.
*   **Uniqueness:** While tradition, reason, and experience are helpful, they are not sources of divine revelation. They are subordinate to the Bible.
*   **The Regulative Principle:** Many Reformed traditions emphasize that we should only worship and practice what is explicitly commanded or exemplified in Scripture.

**Roman Catholic View: *Scripture and Tradition***
The Catholic Church teaches that divine revelation is transmitted through two distinct but connected channels: Sacred Scripture and Sacred Tradition.
*   **Dual Source:** Both are equally valid as modes of divine revelation. Tradition is not just a history of how Scripture has been read; it is the ongoing oral teaching and living transmission of the faith handed down from the Apostles.
*   **The Deposit of Faith:** The "Deposit of Faith" is the totality of revealed truth. It is found partly in written books (Scripture) and partly in unwritten traditions (Tradition) that the Church preserves.

### 2. The Relationship Between the Two

**Reformed View: Tradition is Subordinate**
In Reformed theology, tradition is the "servant" of Scripture.
*   The creeds (Apostles', Nicene) and confessions (Westminster, Heidelberg) are highly respected as summaries of biblical truth.
*   However, if any church council, creed, or tradition contradicts Scripture, the tradition is rejected. The Church creates confessions, but the Bible creates the Church.

**Roman Catholic View: Interdependence**
In Catholic theology, Scripture and Tradition are so closely connected that they cannot be separated.
*   The Church teaches that Scripture *is* part of Tradition (the written part), and Tradition helps interpret Scripture.
*   You cannot fully understand Scripture without the context of Tradition. For example, the doctrines of the Trinity or the exact canon of the Bible are not explicitly detailed in a list within the Bible, yet they are known through Tradition.

questions.response:
The debate between Reformed (Calvinist) and Arminian theologies regarding election centers on **how** and **why** God chooses people for salvation. While both sides agree that God is sovereign and that humans are saved by grace through faith, they fundamentally disagree on the basis of that election and the role of human free will.

Here is a breakdown of the differences.

### 1. The Reformed View: Unconditional Election
Reformed theology, often associated with John Calvin and the "TULIP" acronym, holds to **Unconditional Election**.

*   **The Basis of Election:** God’s choice is based solely on His own sovereign will and good pleasure, not on anything foreseen in the individual. God chooses whom He wills to save out of the mass of sinful humanity.
*   **Foreknowledge:** In this view, God’s "foreknowledge" does not mean He looked down through history to see who would believe and chose them. Rather, it means He intimately knew and set His love upon them *before* time began.
*   **Human Will:** Because humans are "totally depraved" (spiritually dead), they cannot choose God on their own. Therefore, God must first regenerate the heart (give spiritual life) to enable them to believe. Election is the cause of faith, not the result of it.
*   **Key Scripture:** Romans 9:11 ("though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad—in order that God's purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls").

### 2. The Arminian View: Conditional Election
Arminian theology, stemming from Jacobus Arminius and the Remonstrants, holds to **Conditional Election**.

*   **The Basis of Election:** God’s choice is based on His **foreknowledge**. God looks forward through time, sees who will freely place their faith in Christ, and chooses those individuals.
*   **Foreknowledge:** Here, foreknowledge is understood as God knowing in advance what free creatures will do. God elects those whom He foresees will believe.
*   **Human Will:** God grants **prevenient grace** (grace that comes before salvation) to all people, which frees their will from the bondage of sin enough to enable them to accept or reject the Gospel. Election is the result of faith; faith is the cause of election.
*   **Key Scripture:** 1 Peter 1:1-2

*   **Inevitability of Perseverance:** While a believer may stumble into sin or experience seasons of doubt, they will inevitably be brought to repentance. A true Christian cannot "fall away" permanently.
*   **The "False Professor" Explanation:** If a person claims to be a believer, lives like a Christian for a time, and then later renounces the faith and falls away permanently, Reformed theology argues that this person was **never truly regenerated** to begin with. questions.response:
The debate between Reformed paedobaptists (such as Presbyterians) and Reformed Baptists (or credobaptists) is one of the most significant theological distinctives within Protestantism. While both traditions hold to the sovereignty of God, the authority of Scripture, and the doctrines of grace (Calvinism), they diverge sharply on the theology and practice of baptism.

The primary difference lies in how they understand the relationship between the Old and New Covenants, which dictates **who** should be baptized and **what** baptism signifies.

Here is a detailed breakdown of the differences.

### 1. The Subjects of Baptism (Who should be baptized?)

This is the most obvious practical difference.

*   **Reformed Paedobaptists:** Baptize **infants** (and adults) of believing parents. They argue that the children of believers are included in the covenant community and should receive the sign of the covenant.
*   **Reformed Baptists:** Baptize **believers only** (credobaptism). They argue that baptism is exclusively for those who have made a credible profession of faith in Christ.

### 2. The Theological Basis: Covenant Theology

The disagreement over *who* is baptized stems from a disagreement over *how* the Bible fits together (Covenant Theology).

**The Paedobaptist View (Continuity):**
Reformed paedobaptists view the Covenant of Grace as a single, unified promise of salvation running from Genesis to Revelation.
*   They see a strong continuity between the Old and New Testaments.
*   In the Old Testament, the "sign and seal" of entering the covenant was **circumcision**.
*   They point to **Colossians 2:11-12**, which parallels baptism with circumcision ("In him you were also circumcised... having been buried with him in baptism").
*   Therefore, just as infants received the sign of the covenant (circumcision) in the Old Testament, infants of believers should receive the sign of the covenant (baptism) in the New Testament. To exclude children, they argue, would be a regression in God's redemptive plan.

**The Baptist View (Discontinuity):**
Reformed Baptists view the New Covenant as a distinct and "better" covenant (Hebrews 8) that differs in substance from the Old Covenant administrations.
*   They argue that the Old Covenant was a national/ethnic covenant involving physical descendants (the nation of Israel).

questions.response:
The difference between Reformed and Dispensationalist eschatologies stems from a fundamental difference in how they interpret Scripture, particularly the relationship between the Old Testament (Israel) and the New Testament (the Church).

While there are variations within both camps, the primary differences can be categorized into five key areas: **Hermeneutics, Israel vs. the Church, The Kingdom of God, The Millennium, and The Tribulation.**

### 1. Hermeneutics (Interpretation)
The root of the division is not *when* things happen, but *how* we read the Bible.

*   **Reformed (Covenantal):** Uses a **"Redemptive-Historical"** or **"Christocentric"** approach. They believe the New Testament provides the lens through which the Old Testament must be understood. They view prophecy as often symbolic, typological, or conditional ("spiritualizing"). If the New Testament interprets an Old Testament prophecy about Israel as applying to Jesus or the Church, the Reformed reader accepts that fulfillment.
*   **Dispensationalist:** Uses a **"Literal"** (or plain-sense) approach. They prioritize the grammatical-historical meaning of the text at the time it was written. They generally argue that prophecies made to national Israel must be fulfilled literally for national Israel, unless the text itself explicitly dictates a metaphorical meaning. They resist "spiritualizing" prophecies about the land, the temple, or the throne.

### 2. Israel and the Church
This is the most significant theological divide.

*   **Reformed:** Believes in the **unity of the people of God**. They hold that the Church is the continuation of "True Israel." Abraham’s physical descendants who rejected Christ were cut off (like branches pruned from a tree), and Gentiles who believe are grafted in (Romans 11). Therefore, most Old Testament promises to Israel are spiritually fulfilled in the Church (the "Israel of God").
*   **Dispensationalist:** Believes in a **sharp distinction** between Israel and the Church. They view them as two distinct peoples of God with distinct destinies. Israel is an earthly people with earthly promises (the land, the throne), while the Church is a heavenly people (a "mystery" not revealed in the Old Testament). They argue that God has not finished with ethnic Israel and will fulfill His Old Testament promises to them literally in the future.
